html:
A merchant and banker of Surat, the main Mughal port on the west coast of India, who lived from about 1590 to the 1670s. English records called him the richest merchant in the world.

He was a Jain trader with agents across India and around the Indian Ocean, from the Persian Gulf to Southeast Asia. He often bought up whole cargoes of spices, coral or other goods arriving at Surat, then set the price for resale. He dealt in pepper, cardamom, cloth, bullion and much else.

The new European companies needed him. Both the English East India Company and the Dutch East India Company borrowed from him and bought and sold through him; sometimes they were partners, sometimes rivals. His career shows that Indian merchant capital and credit networks, such as the sarafs and their hundi bills, were at least the equal of the Europeans in the 17th century.

In 1664 Shivaji's Maratha forces sacked Surat and plundered his house, but his business went on.
